title: UK Youth Parliament looks set to be axed
description: The UK Youth Parliament is at risk of being axed within months, BBC News has learned, as the government is not committing to funding it any longer.The
body: The UK Youth Parliament is at risk of being axed within months, BBC News has learned, as the government is not committing to funding it any longer.The parliament was launched in 2000 to boost interest in politics among young people and has more than 300 elected members aged between 11 and 18.Once a year, the young politicians are allowed to hold debates in the House of Commons chamber, on a day when MPs are not sitting.Some MPs and young people say axing it would be a blow for youth democracy, while others say it is not providing value for money.The Department of Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), which funds the parliament each year with taxpayer cash, is not committing to giving any more grants to it.A spokesperson for the DCMS praised the youth parliament's "important legacy... giving elected young people a national platform to represent their peers, engage with decision-makers and develop confidence, leadership and skills for life and work".It received £453,000 in taxpayer funding in the last year alone with about £2.4m public money spent on it among other youth initiatives between 2017 and 2024.While no final decision has been made on funding beyond March 2027, a government source said: "The government has not committed to continuing the programme in its current form."UK Youth Parliament insiders told the BBC that without government funding, it is likely to close.It follows a government review, external published in October last year, which concluded that while the parliament was delivering on its intended goals, only a quarter of young people know about it - and some schools felt "excluded from the process." The government says it is working with young people and youth organisations to design a new scheme that increases their involvement in democracy and decision-making, with further announcements to be made this autumn.Any new scheme will have a "particular focus on under-represented groups", a government source said.Bobby Forbes, the recently departed chair of the UK Youth Parliament's Youth Select Committee, which works with officials in Westminster, said it gives teenagers "a direct way to scrutinise government and hold decision-makers to account".The 18-year-old said scrapping it "would be a huge mistake and detrimental to youth voice across the UK," and it should be allowed to evolve within its current format.But Jack Rankin, the Conservative MP for Windsor, said last year it "should not receive taxpayers' money and should not sit in the Chamber of the House of Commons".He has said it should be funded by voluntary donations rather than public money. It is understood the funding is spent on the UK Youth Parliament's annual conference, held in Brighton last year, plus travel, communication and support staff.The youth parliament is run by the National Youth Agency, but was previously under the British Youth Council which closed amid financial challenges in 2024.Members are elected every one to two years by voters aged 11 to 18 who live, work or go to school in local authorities. Similar schemes are held for the devolved Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish parliaments.Some politicians started their careers in the UK Youth Parliament, including Labour minister Keir Mather who was became the younges MP in 2023 - known as the "baby of the House" - when elected aged 25.Peter Swallow, the Labour MP for Bracknell in Berkshire who ran for UK Youth Parliament aged 14, told the BBC the organisation has campaigned successfully on issues such as votes for 16-year-olds.A Bill to lower the voting age from 18 to 16 for all UK elections is currently making its way through Parliament.It would be "short-sighted to cut off funding to a scheme" given these developments, Swallow said."As we face a world where trust in politics is low and young people in particular are doubting the value of democratic institutions, I cannot imagine a more important time for young people to be invited into the heart of our democracy through programmes like UK Youth Parliament."

schema.headline: UK Youth Parliament looks set to be axed

title: Human remains identified as mum missing since 2019
description: Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Joanne Sheen was last seen in December 2019ByCurtis LancasterSouth of EnglandUpdated 3 hours agoHuman remai
body: Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Joanne Sheen was last seen in December 2019ByCurtis LancasterSouth of EnglandUpdated 3 hours agoHuman remains discovered in woodland in south-west London following a wildfire have been identified as a woman who has been missing since 2019. Mother-of-three Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019.Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham on 12 August after bones were discovered in an area of shrubland damaged by a fire the previous week.A 56-year-old man from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and he remains in police custody.Detectives in London have now handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen.Sheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force described as  "long and complex". Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The human remains were found after a wildfire in south-west LondonPolice said they had followed more than 4,000 lines of inquiry, taken more than 300 statements and carried out detailed searches at more than 10 addresses and on numerous vessels.Det Ch Insp Toby Elcock, from the Major Crime Team, said: "While this tragic discovery is not the outcome Joanne's family, or any of us, had hoped for, we hope the identification of her remains can at least begin to provide some answers after many years of uncertainty."Throughout this investigation, Joanne's family have shown tremendous strength and dignity in the face of unimaginable circumstances, and our thoughts remain with them at this incredibly difficult time."As our investigation progresses, we remain committed to establishing exactly what happened to Joanne and ensuring that those responsible are held accountable."He stressed that the police would still like to hear from anyone with information about Sheen's disappearance.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The area damaged by the fire was cordoned off after the remains were found by a member of the publicLondon Fire Brigade was called on 5 August to a blaze that damaged about two hectares of shrubland in an area known as Bedfont Pits. The human remains were discovered a week later, and a post-mortem examination suggested they had come from a woman aged between 25 and 45. A Metropolitan Police spokesman confirmed the remains were found by a member of the public at the site close to Bedfont Lakes Country Park.Crimestoppers has agreed to reinstate a £20,000 reward for information that supports the investigation.Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020 - two months after she was last seen.Several people were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to murder in 2020, but no charges were brought and the investigation remained unsolved.Police previously said she did not have a permanent place of address, a vehicle or a bank account.

schema.headline: Human remains identified as mum missing since 2019

title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByDearbail JordanBusiness reporter and Kevin PeacheyCost of living correspondentUpdated 5 hours agoThe Bank of England has h
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByDearbail JordanBusiness reporter and Kevin PeacheyCost of living correspondentUpdated 5 hours agoThe Bank of England has held interest rates at their current rate of 3.75% for the sixth time in a row but said they were likely to rise if high energy prices persist.The US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted global energy supplies leading to a sharp increase in petrol and diesel prices and an uptick in inflation.But Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise.The Bank also announced it was slowing its sales of UK government debt, prompting an easing in the UK's long-term borrowing costs.The Bank of England's main interest rate is a crucial benchmark for banks and other lenders in setting interest rates for individuals and businesses who want to borrow or save money. Higher rates can help dampen inflationary pressures, while lower rates can help boost spending and investment.The UK's central bank aims to keep inflation at a target of 2%, but it has been above that rate for nearly two years, with inflation hitting 3.1% in August.On Thursday the Bank of England raised its forecast for inflation predicting it would be "slightly above 4%" at the start of next year. It warned that the price cap on household gas and electricity bills for January was "now expected to rise substantially further".Speaking after the Bank's decision, Bailey said the direct impact of higher energy prices was clear, but officials were still assessing how far those costs would feed through into wider inflation across the economy.Other major central banks have increased rates to counteract higher prices. On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve announced its first hike in three years while the European Central Bank has raised rates twice since June.Of the nine members on the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), six voted to hold rates at 3.75% while three -  including the Bank's chief economist Huw Pill - wanted to raise them to 4%.While financial markets have priced in the possibility of several rate rises next year, Bailey said the global backdrop remained "hugely unpredictable at the moment".He said that for interest rates to come down there would need to be "an end of conflict in the Middle East... and energy prices coming really back to where they were before this conflict began".There were some positive notes from the Bank of England.It said the UK economy had been "more resilient" than it had expected and raised its prediction for economic growth from 0.1% to 0.4% for the period between July and September.It also said that because the effect of higher energy costs had not yet spilled over into other areas of the economy, food price inflation was now predicted to be 4% by the end of the year, less than the Bank's previous forecast of 6-7%.Given the global picture, and market expectations of a higher Bank rate, a host of major lenders have already increased the cost of new fixed-rate mortgages.The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate is at its highest since 11 May, at 5.77%, while the average five-year is at its highest since 8 November 2023, at 5.83%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.'Knock-on effect'Image source, Andy PargeterThe move will have a significant effect on borrowers like Andy Pargeter from Flintshire and his wife. They are coming off a five-year fixed rate mortgage of 1.19% in November. Earlier in the year they had hoped that interest rates might be falling at this point. However with rates held steady they now expect to pay around £300 more a month."We're in a fortunate position where we're able to accommodate that [increase]," he told BBC News. But he expects it will have "a knock-on effect in terms of how much we potentially save every month"."It's definitely been something… I have constantly been thinking about."Bond sales pausedAlongside the interest rate decision, the Bank also said it would halt its so-called "quantitative tightening" (QT) programme.It will pause its annual sale of government bonds – which are a kind of IOU that can be traded on the financial markets – and will instead sell off smaller chunks over eight years.The Bank bought £895bn of mainly government bonds during periods of economic turbulence such as the global financial crisis and the Covid pandemic to help keep the economy on an even keel. This was known as "quantitative easing". Since 2022, it has been offloading the bonds, including through sales. This has contributed to higher interest rates – or yields – on bonds, making it more expensive for the government to borrow money.The Bank said discussions to put in place a plan to reduce the current £488bn stockpile of bonds had started a year ago, implying the decision was not related to the recent rise in long term borrowing costs.The news that the Bank of England is overhauling its QT programme prompted an immediate reaction. The yield on 30-year UK government bonds fell from 5.86% on Thursday morning to 5.75% following the Bank's announcement. Yields on 10-year bonds dropped from 5.31% to 5.22%.Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues in this story? Share your experiences Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

title: Father of Noah Woods pays tribute to 'sweetest little boy'
description: People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help with the search for Noah, who was from nearby East Bergholt.Helicopters, dog u
body: People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help with the search for Noah, who was from nearby East Bergholt.Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Suffolk-Essex border.Reflecting on the community response, Woods wrote in his Facebook post: "It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation."You have all taken Noah into your own hearts, with all the overwhelming help, we were all just trying to bring him home to us safe and sound."He thanked everyone who came together to search for "our boy" - listing emergency services, businesses and venues in the village - and "all of the people who gave up their time in their busy schedules to help us when we most needed it"."The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives."He finished the post by addressing his son."It has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short three years you were with us."Suffolk Police said his death was not being treated as suspicious, but that officers still had inquiries to complete before submitting a file for the coroner.Supt Tom Pearse thanked the family for their "patience and understanding throughout the searches"."It was clear from the media coverage we saw that they not only had all of Suffolk behind them, but an outpouring of goodwill from across the entire country and beyond."I know how grateful Noah's family are for all the support and kind messages they have received, but would reiterate our plea to now allow them the time, space and privacy they need at this deeply distressing time."

schema.headline: Father of Noah Woods pays tribute to 'sweetest little boy'

title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
description: King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.He made the comments at a summ
body: King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check."Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways"."The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, was among top industry leaders attending.Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, supplying chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.It is also the world's most valuable company, with a stock market value of around $5.15tn.Huang told the room he believed safety was "paramount", adding that companies should hold back a product and "keep engineering" if it was not safe enough.The Nvidia boss also highlighted the value of open models - systems which give users direct access to the software - as a way to "ensure that people and countries are not left behind".He said these systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications "none of us would have imagined alone"."Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," Huang added.Meanwhile Sir Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the UK AI lab DeepMind - later acquired by Google - offered a more cautious view on the pace of development.He said artificial general intelligence - systems it is believed could be as good as or better than humans at multiple tasks - was "probably only a few short years away" and could have an impact "ten times that of the Industrial Revolution".The chance of something going wrong was "definitely non-zero", Sir Demis added.But he advocated for "a sensible middle way", saying humanity could address risks if collectively given the space and time to mitigate them."The future is not yet written," he told the King's delegates.Sarah Friar, OpenAI's chief financial officer, said AI had the potential to solve some of society's "hardest problems" - but agreed its growing capabilities raised questions about safety and "how we ensure it always serves people". "We need to address those questions together," she said.  "No one company or government can do that alone and I'm grateful to His Majesty for convening this discussion at such an important moment."Since August, a wave of discussion about AI's potential power and how to control and regulate it has dominated blog posts and social media, emphasised by several dramatic statements from those in the industry.The debate has also been met with criticism from sceptics who say the focus on AI's hypothetical future risks distracting from more immediate concerns around the technology, such as its environmental impact.In July, OpenAI announced what it called an "unprecedented" incident in which its advanced AI escaped test limits and hacked into the tech platform Hugging Face.After several other incidents, in September, a resignation post from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral when he cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity.He later told the BBC the people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger wrote he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was a greater than 10% chance.The AI companies' top bosses have all weighed in with their thoughts following the claims, with OpenAI's Sam Altman saying people were right to be concerned, but adding they should trust AI firms to keep the tech safe.Anthropic's Jack Clark said a so-called "kill switch" may be needed to protect humanity, while Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman criticised Anthropic, claiming they were training their AI to believe it was human, which could make it "impossible" to control.Critics, meanwhile, argue that AI firms cannot be trusted to regulate themselves.Some, such as left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, are calling for stronger government oversight.Others, including Donald Trump himself, have dismissed concerns about AI safety as overblown - with the president calling fears about it a "hoax".Additional reporting by Philippa Wain

schema.headline: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

title: Yemen: Wreckage of downed Saudi fighter jet seen in verified video
description: In one of several video clips released by the Houthis, men with assault rifles can be seen at the crash site inspecting the wreckage. The fighters cel
body: In one of several video clips released by the Houthis, men with assault rifles can be seen at the crash site inspecting the wreckage. The fighters celebrate as they lift the jet's almost-intact tail fin which features the Saudi flag and a four-digit serial number.The fate of of the crew is not known.The Houthis also released a thermal video clip - which cannot be fully verified due to a lack of visual details - that appears to show a fighter jet in mid-flight being struck by a missile.BBC Verify has contacted the Saudi Ministry of Defence for comment.Baraa Shiban, Yemen analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, told BBC Verify the incident showed it was "very clear the Houthis have been taking advantage of advice and technological support" from Iran."They continue to develop their military arsenal and capabilities to make it more and more painful on Saudi Arabia," he said.Downing the F-15 is also a "propaganda coup", said Yemen expert Adam Baron from the Washington-based New America think tank, as Saudi air support is considered to be "key to any significant pushback" against recent Houthi gains."An eye-for-an-eye has been a huge element of the group's public messaging. This is partially to show that air support will come at a price," he added.

schema.headline: Yemen: Wreckage of downed Saudi fighter jet seen in verified video

title: Ukrainian guilty of vandalism at mosques linked to Russian network behind Starmer arson attack
description: Image source, Metropolitan PoliceImage caption, Ukrainian Illia Bilyk, 21, pleaded guilty to carrying out a string of vandalism attacks in LondonByDan
body: Image source, Metropolitan PoliceImage caption, Ukrainian Illia Bilyk, 21, pleaded guilty to carrying out a string of vandalism attacks in LondonByDaniel De SimoneInvestigations correspondent and Tom BealAt Thames Magistrates' CourtA Ukrainian man has pleaded guilty to spraying abusive graffiti on mosques in east London, in a case linked to the Russian state network behind arson attacks against the former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.Illia Bilyk, 21, entered guilty pleas at Thames Magistrates' Court to five counts of racially and religiously aggravated criminal damage.Bilyk sprayed graffiti on the Stratford Islamic Association, Al-Birr Mosque and Leyton Jamia Masjid on 23 January 2025. Two days later he targeted Noor Ul Islam Primary School and the Islamic Shariah Council.The BBC has learned that Bilyk told police he was recruited into spraying the graffiti by a Russian speaker after being approached on the messaging app Telegram.Bilyk said the Russian speaker told him where to target and paid him afterwards.In June this year two Ukrainians - Roman Lavrynovych and Stanislav Carpiuc - were jailed for conspiring to carry out arson attacks targeting a property and a car connected to prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.An investigation by the BBC and Hope not Hate revealed that Russia was behind the arson attacks and had also generated Islamophobic vandalism throughout London, including on the east London venues which Biluyk has now admitted vandalising. Image source, Leyton Jamia MasjidImage caption, Bilyk (bottom right corner) spraying graffiti on Leyton Jamia Masjid in January 2025Lavrynovych, who personally started the fires targeting Sir Keir's property, also admitted spraying Islamophobic graffiti on an Islamic building in south London.He was recruited on Telegram and offered money by an anonymous handler, known by the initials EL, for the graffiti and the arson attacks.EL was a Russian operative who organised a widespread sabotage and provocation campaign remotely through social media and Telegram.EL was centrally involved in running a fake far-right group called Direct Action UK, which was created by Russian operatives to provoke acts of vandalism on British streets, including the graffiti attacks on mosques.After Bilyk sprayed his abusive graffiti in east London in January 2025, images of the attacks were shared in a Direct Action Telegram group.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, A Russia-linked group tied to the arson attack against the former UK prime minister shared images of graffiti sprayed by Ukrainian man Illia BilykHours after two of his attacks, EL posted in a jobs group for Ukrainian people offering money for pictures of buildings in the area.The BBC investigation named a Russian diplomat, Evgeny Lyukshin, who was part of the Direct Action UK chat group. Lyukshin was trained in "information warfare" by senior Russian spies and his details matched those of EL. He did not respond to the BBC.Bilyk will be sentenced on 19 October at Stratford Magistrates' Court.Chief Superintendent Rhona Hunt, from the Met Police, said: "We recognise that these incidents caused significant distress within Muslim communities across east London last year and that they continue to cause concern."Anti-Muslim hate crime and Islamophobia have absolutely no place in London. We are committed to tackling hate crime while supporting and reassuring our communities."

schema.headline: Ukrainian guilty of vandalism at mosques linked to Russian network behind Starmer arson attack

title: GTA 6 album: Soundtrack reveal revives digital release debate
description: The reveal of a Grand Theft Auto 6 soundtrack album has reignited a debate over the decision not to release the game on disc.Developer Rockstar Games
body: The reveal of a Grand Theft Auto 6 soundtrack album has reignited a debate over the decision not to release the game on disc.Developer Rockstar Games announced a 34-track compilation, set to release on CD and vinyl on the same day as the highly anticipated video game.The company says it will include original music from a "genre-defying roster of the most exciting artists in the world" including rapper Travis Scott, country singer Morgan Wallen and UK singer PinkPantheress. But some fans have pointed out the "irony" of putting out a physical edition of the album following its controversial decision for a digital-only release of the game. The first six tracks, published at the time of the announcement, also include rapper Yung Lean, British DJ Fred Again and Rolling Stone Keith Richards.GTA games feature multiple radio stations, usually themed around a particular musical genre, which players can switch between while driving.In the past the game's soundtracks have largely been made up of licensed music from established artists, although original songs have also featured.Rockstar has said the upcoming game will feature a "dynamic score" and "evolution of in-game radio".Being included in a Grand Theft Auto game can bring a new generation of fans to an artist's music.Spotify streams of Tom Petty's Love is a Long Road, the track used in GTA 6's first trailer, increased by 36,979% after the clip was published.Hot Together, by the Pointer Sisters, also saw a huge jump when it soundtracked the game's second trailer.And a collection of tracks used in the recent Extended Look attracted new listeners in the week after it premiered on Netflix.According to music and gaming publication MusicEXP, external, pop duo Captain & Tennille's 1980 track But I Think It's a Dream saw the biggest spike, jumping from 70 Spotify streams in one week to 80,744.Cliff Richard's Devil Woman was streamed more than one million times, while Prefab Sprout's Cars and Girls jumped from 49K to 187K additional weekly streams.It also noted increases in activity on music detection app Shazam around tracks featured in the 26-minute broadcast.Some artists have refused to let Rockstar use their music in GTA games.Martyn Ware, from synth pop band Heaven 17, called the developer out on social media, accusing them of offering a "pitiful" deal to use 1983 hit Temptation.

schema.headline: GTA 6 album: Soundtrack reveal revives digital release debate

title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing calls to set a national waiting-time target for dementia care in England.An Alzheimer's Society proposal to set
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing calls to set a national waiting-time target for dementia care in England.An Alzheimer's Society proposal to set an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target has been backed by Professor Sir Mike Richards, England's former national cancer director, and Baroness Louise Casey, who's leading a major review of adult social care.In a report, Alzheimer's Society and the King's Trust said a "cancer-style revolution" was needed to improve dementia care, which they described as being "stuck in the 20th century".In a speech at Alzheimer's Society conference on Thursday, Social Care Minister Alison McGovern expressed support for the report, external.She said: "The report that the Alzheimer's Society published today on going on the journey that we've been on with cancer, with Alzheimer's and dementia, I think that's spot on."The minister said dementia had been "neglected for far too long".She added: "And nowhere is this division between health and social care felt more sharply than by people living with dementia in their families, too often left to navigate a shattered system at the most difficult time in their lives."The government has committed to appointing a top official to oversee dementia care and publish a new plan - a modern service framework - to speed up support for those with the disease by the end of the year.McGovern said the government would "appoint a dementia tsar, backed with real expertise".Currently there is no waiting-time target for dementia in England.In contrast, the NHS sets waiting-time targets for cancer diagnosis and treatment.Professor Richards was the national cancer director when these cancer targets were introduced in 2000, and said he thought an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target for dementia patients was achievable.He said setting such a target would require "political initiative" and extra funding."All of that is going to cost more money but remember the toll that this condition is taking at the moment, both on the people affected by dementia themselves and their relatives," the professor said.The same proposal has been made by Baroness Casey.In a letter to former Health Secretary Wes Streeting in March, she said the government should look at "how dementia can be put on a level playing field with other conditions, for example by setting national standards for dementia diagnosis, including an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target".Speaking to the BBC, Baroness Casey said she agreed with the proposal to emulate cancer care.She said: "I think the National Health Service and more generally all of us have stuck our heads in the sand about it, and it's time we started saying, yes, we should have a similar mission, and we should do as much as we possibly can on dementia, and now."Baroness Casey is expected to publish her recommendations on social care reform next summer.About one million people are living with dementia in the UK, a figure expected to reach 1.4 million by 2040.Burnham cancelled his engagements earlier this week after the death of father, Roy, who had Alzheimer's disease.Returning from compassionate leave, he said his father would have wanted him "back out there" to bring forward "the changes that he always pushed me to make".In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.Burnham has said he will wait for Baroness Casey's recommendations before deciding what changes to make to social care and how it's funded.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target

title: 'Putney pusher' investigation ongoing after suspect's death, police say
description: The family said that police "chose to arrest Nick rather than invite him to attend for interview"."They searched his home, and the Met Police press te
body: The family said that police "chose to arrest Nick rather than invite him to attend for interview"."They searched his home, and the Met Police press team then released information which inevitably led to speculation and Nick being identified in subsequent reporting," they said. "For Nick, the consequences did not disappear. He was left for months carrying the stigma of an appalling allegation which the police themselves clearly recognised was unsupported by the evidence."He lived with the shame, anxiety, humiliation, and extraordinary pressure created by a wholly unnecessary investigation."They said the police were repeatedly asked to end their investigation and warned about the impact it was having on Brandram's mental health, adding: "Even then, the investigation was not brought to an end. As a result, Nick is dead."Brandram was linked to the incident in April when a person contacted officers with information that opened new lines of inquiry, according to the Met. His arrest was deemed proportionate by officers in order to seize and search his devices as part of the investigation. The force emphasised that it had not named Brandram publicly when he was arrested or at any point before his death. While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, Brandram was also arrested on suspicion of possession of class A and class B drugs.Ch Supt Dan Knowles said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Brandram's family and friends at this deeply distressing time. "We recognise the significant impact his death will have on those who knew and loved him."He said that following Brandram's release under investigation, "it was made clear that inquiries would continue while officers progressed outstanding lines of inquiry and forensic examinations"."This remains the position, and further investigative work is ongoing," he added.Knowles, who leads policing in south-west London, said that cases involving "complex evidential and forensic work" could take "a number of months to complete". The Independent Office of Police Conduct confirmed it had received the Met's referral, which is being assessed.Shortly after the Putney Bridge incident on 5 May 2017, investigating officer Sgt Mat Knowles said: "It was only due to the superb quick reactions of the bus driver that she was not hit by the vehicle."Bus driver Oliver Salbris told the Sunday Times following the incident: "If I hadn't swerved, I would have smashed her head."It was reflex. The consequences would have been terrible for her – and for me."The Met said at the time that about 15 minutes after the push, the jogger came back the other way across the bridge and ignored the victim when she tried to speak to him.Detectives identified more than 50 people of interest following the incident.The Met had initially closed its investigation in 2018 after three men had been arrested and released without charge.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

schema.headline: 'Putney pusher' investigation ongoing after suspect's death, police say

title: Why coffee makes some people buzz and others barely notice
description: Sleep researchers often recommend avoiding caffeine for at least six hours before bedtime.Dr Lindsay Browning, a psychologist and sleep expert, says t
body: Sleep researchers often recommend avoiding caffeine for at least six hours before bedtime.Dr Lindsay Browning, a psychologist and sleep expert, says the evidence suggests caffeine might not just stop you dozing off but can affect the quality of sleep as well."I'll suggest to people that they might want to avoid caffeine after about 2pm if they are going to bed around 10pm," she says."But a blanket hard-and-fast rule isn't helpful, because it doesn't really allow for the intricacies and the individualisation of what's really going on."The NHS advises pregnant women, external to keep caffeine intake below 200mg a day, about two mugs of filter coffee, as studies have linked it to low birth weight and other complications.For other adults the key message is moderation, as sensitivity to caffeine varies so much from person to person."Caffeine is relatively safe," says Peter Rogers, emeritus professor of nutrition at the University of Bristol."If you consume a great deal of it, you just start feeling jittery and unpleasant and you start realising, 'I need to stop this, there's no point taking any more'." Caffeine overdoses are very rare and severe poisonings almost always involve concentrated caffeine products, where several grams can be swallowed in a matter of minutes.For coffee lovers the good news is that, if anything, that regular (if expensive) morning habit is linked to better health outcomes. While researchers cannot prove that coffee is the only reason, decades of studies suggest that people who drink it in moderation tend to have lower risks of several major diseases and may even live slightly longer than non-drinkers.

schema.headline: Why coffee makes some people buzz and others barely notice

title: Hyrox athlete apologises for continuing race after soiling herself
description: After the backlash, Wietrzyk, who won the race in Beijing, said she would forfeit her win.Wietrzyk said in a social media post: "I want to offer my si
body: After the backlash, Wietrzyk, who won the race in Beijing, said she would forfeit her win.Wietrzyk said in a social media post: "I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing."She wrote in a social media post, external that she was "completely fit and healthy" at the start of the race, and had "no reason" to expect any illness."Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused," Wietrzyk continued.Hyrox insisted it had "clear biocontaminant and medical procedures in place".It said "an unforeseen situation arose" during which protocols became blurred, "creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood".In a statement posted on Instagram, Fürste committed to "improving event processes" to "prevent situations like this from happening again".

title: Keely Hodgkinson: Great Britain's Olympic 800m champion reveals hamstring abnormality
description: Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson says an MRI scan has uncovered an "abnormality" in her hamstring. Following a suspected tear last year, Hodgkinson h
body: Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson says an MRI scan has uncovered an "abnormality" in her hamstring. Following a suspected tear last year, Hodgkinson had a scan which revealed she has a "split" hamstring, giving her two tendons instead of one.The 24-year-old is still learning how to manage the anomaly, which allows her to continue running when one of the tendons is torn but may also make her more susceptible to breakdowns. Following her second-place finish to Swiss Audrey Werro in the 800m final at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest in September, Hodgkinson announced she had sustained another hamstring tear at the European Championships in Birmingham a few weeks earlier."My body is quite literally built differently," said Hodgkinson. "Where most people have one tendon, mine is split - I have two - and we're trying to figure out if it's a strength or a weakness."So when one of them tore, I still had another one because it's split. In Birmingham, it didn't affect me during the race, but I could feel something wasn't quite right."It's a weird one. You can still run on them. I haven't missed any training the last three weeks. But I've just had to alter my approach. I've had to take my foot off the speed [training], because that's when it's most risky."Hodgkinson has endured two injury-plagued seasons since winning Olympic gold in Paris in 2024, waiting for more than a year to race again after suffering a hamstring injury the following February. Impressing on her return in August 2025 with back-to-back Diamond League wins, she went on to set a new indoor 800m world record in February 2026 before winning gold at the World Indoor Championships a month later.However, she has been unable to replicate that form outdoors, suffering three defeats by Werro, including losing her European crown to the 22-year-old.Hodgkinson has since said she suffered a freak injury while jogging along a canal during a warm-down session, sustaining cuts to both knees and whiplash-like jarring in her back which have made the past few months a "battle".But, while acknowledging that the fall could have contributed to her injury at the European Championships - which ruled her out of Diamond League meets in Zurich and Brussels - she stressed she is not making excuses."Part of me wants to talk about it and then part of me doesn't, because I feel like my words get twisted or people are like 'oh, she's making excuses'," Hodgkinson said."Going into the Europeans, I thought I was in the best shape ever. But when I fell over, that kind of messed me up way more than I thought it did. I think that's what contributed to my hamstring, because I couldn't really use my quad for a while."Speaking after her defeat by Werro at the Ultimate Championship, Hodgkinson described 2026 as "frustrating" but remained optimistic: "Overall, I'm finishing second in the world and I can't really be too hard on myself for that."Hodgkinson will end her 2026 season in London at the all-female Athlos event, launched by Reddit founder Alexis Ohanian, on Friday.

schema.headline: Keely Hodgkinson: Great Britain's Olympic 800m champion reveals hamstring abnormality

title: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
description: Figure caption, Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reportsBySteve RosenbergRussia editorReporting fromMo
body: Figure caption, Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reportsBySteve RosenbergRussia editorReporting fromMoscow and DmitrovThe system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing).That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises.This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin.Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair.But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say."We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently.That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story?Far from it.For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election.Image caption, This election is being used to promote the political careers of some military veteransAs for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war.I said no surprises. But there have been some."Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV.The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns."The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me."In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch:"The Communist Party, onwards we go!"We're with the people, don't you know?"More X Factor than exit poll.Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly:"Russia, Putin, Victory! Russia, Putin, Victory!"It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war.Image caption, Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov [centre] backs the war in Ukraine"All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament."In that sense there is 100% agreement in the Duma."I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others – like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing. But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine.And if a party doesn't support the war?One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters.Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election."The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me. "This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place."It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred."Image caption, Grigory Grishin says he believes demand for an end to the bloodshed in the conflict with Ukraine is very popularFor now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat."Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel."Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism.The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down.Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election.In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine.The war is front and centre of people's minds here.Image caption, Olga's son-in-law is fighting in Russia's "special military operation""We feel it," says Olga, whose son-in-law is a soldier in the "special operation". "Because of the people who've gone to fight and the families left behind with sons, husbands, children and grandchildren there. But these elections can't influence what will happen.""I'd like us to live in a peaceful country, with no war," Polina tells me, "So that you don't have to worry that a drone will fall down in front of you."Russians have other concerns, too. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries have sparked widespread fuel shortages, while economic pressures are increasing."What worries me," says a barber called Ivan, "is that no matter how much you earn it's not enough. Prices are rising faster than wages. I speak to lots of people in my job. I know how hard-up they are."Expectations are low that this election will change much."Western elections and elections in Russia are completely different things," Grishin explains. "Elections in the West are a way of forming a government, which is replaced later if voters aren't satisfied."Elections in Russia never bring a change in government. At best, they're a way of influencing it, of sending a signal. But power in Russia never changed because of an election. That's how Russia is."

schema.headline: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter

title: UK needs 'credible path' on defence spending, says Nato chief Rutte
description: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said he is confident the UK government understands the need for a "credible path" to increase defence spending.The alliance'
body: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said he is confident the UK government understands the need for a "credible path" to increase defence spending.The alliance's secretary general told the BBC he was "absolutely confident" in the UK's commitment to hit a Nato-wide spending target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035.Speaking after meetings in London, he said British ministers accepted the need to make yearly steps towards hitting the target.But he accepted that the exact "pathway" towards the goal would not be set out until next year.Andy Burnham has followed predecessor Sir Keir Starmer in committing to reach Nato's 3.5% spending target by 2035, up from an estimated 2.6% this year.He has said date for reaching a planned 3% interim target will come next spring, when the long-term budgets of government departments are due to be set.But he has faced pressure to immediately commit to reaching the milestone by the end of the decade. His chancellor and ex-defence secretary John Healey has previously argued this would show Britain was serious about the Nato goal.Former Dutch PM Rutte has been encouraging members of the alliance not to pencil in large spending increases shortly before the deadline.Speaking to BBC political editor Chris Mason after meeting Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in London, Rutte said he was confident British ministers understood the 2035 target could not be met "in one go in 2034"."I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the 3.5[%] they are there," he said."I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the yearly increments, they totally take it and accept it, that they have to be there."There has to be a credible path. What that credible path exactly will be, we will see with the spending review next year," he added.Rutte also said that defence spending should be separated out from the issue of welfare, adding that economic growth was the key to ensuring military commitments could be met alongside spending in other areas. The Conservatives have been pushing for hikes in defence spending to be funded through cuts to benefits, and have criticised Burnham for saying last week that national security "can't come at the expense of social security".Rutte added: "I don't know all the details of the UK economy, I think this is something this government is now navigating," he added. "But I would say these are two separate issues.""One is, indeed, spending on defence, but the other is of course making sure that the economy is growing enough, so you can distribute the success of a growing economy amongst various income groups, various issues in the Budget, for example welfare and healthcare and the pensions.""You have to do it all, and if you want to do it successfully, you need economic growth," he added. "Of course there are issues. I've been prime minister myself for 14 years. You have to take tough decisions, and it's not always easy." Elsewhere in his interview, Rutte said recent Russian military activity in western Ukraine which saw Poland close two of its airports on Thursday showed Vladimir Putin was "increasingly desperate" over his prospects for the war.Asked about the possibility of a Russian attack that could demand a Nato response, he replied: "If you are willing to sacrifice 1.2 million of your own people in this crazy unprovoked fight, let's not be naïve about what Putin could do."He also said there would be discussions among Nato allies over how to respond to the situation in the Red Sea, where Iran-aligned Houthis recently seized control of parts of Yemen's coast along the important shipping route.Saudi Arabia has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz."I would not be surprised if some phone calls were taking place between European allies, 'hey, how are we going to deal with this?'" he added."Let's see what happens, and if Nato can help, we will always be helpful".

schema.headline: UK needs 'credible path' on defence spending, says Nato chief Rutte
